presidents.name: Ronald Reagan
presidents.summary: Reagan signed the law making Martin Luther King, Jr.'s birthday a federal holiday in 1983 and signed the Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986, which set mandatory minimum drug penalties at what the U.S. Sentencing Commission later called the 100-to-1 crack-to-powder cocaine quantity ratio. He vetoed the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 and the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987; Congress overrode both vetoes.
presidents.paragraph: Two of Reagan's most-cited actions on race point in opposite directions, and both are on the record in the Statutes at Large. On November 2, 1983 he signed Public Law 98-144, adding "Birthday of Martin Luther King, Jr., the third Monday in January" to the federal holiday list, and he spoke at the signing with Coretta Scott King present. Three years later, on October 27, 1986, he signed Public Law 99-570, the Anti-Drug Abuse Act, whose text set the five-year mandatory minimum at 5 grams of cocaine base but 500 grams of powder, and the ten-year minimum at 50 grams versus 5,000 — the ratio the U.S. Sentencing Commission's 2007 report to Congress describes as the "100-to-1 drug quantity ratio." He also vetoed two bills Congress then enacted over his objection: the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 (vetoed September 26, 1986; House overrode September 29, Senate October 2) and the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987 (vetoed March 16, 1988; both chambers overrode March 22).

disputes: Reagan's stated reason for vetoing the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act was that broad sanctions would harm Black South Africans and impede a peaceful end to apartheid; the congressional majority that overrode the veto held the opposite view of sanctions' effect. The record shows both positions; this file does not resolve which was correct.

Whether the 100-to-1 crack/powder ratio in the 1986 Act was intended to target Black defendants, or produced that effect without that intent, is contested in the scholarly literature. The U.S. Sentencing Commission's reports document the disparate racial impact but the question of legislative intent is not settled by the sources fetched here.

presidents.name: George H. W. Bush
presidents.summary: Bush vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1990 on October 22, 1990, and the Senate failed to override it two days later by 66-34. He signed a renegotiated bill, the Civil Rights Act of 1991, on November 21, 1991, and nominated Clarence Thomas to the Supreme Court, who was confirmed 52-48 on October 15, 1991.
presidents.paragraph: Bush's civil rights record turns on a two-year fight over employment discrimination law. On October 22, 1990 he returned S. 2104, the Civil Rights Act of 1990, to the Senate without his approval, writing that he deeply regretted acting against a bill with that title. The Senate's override attempt failed 66-34 on October 24, 1990. A year later he signed a renegotiated version: Public Law 102-166, the Civil Rights Act of 1991, enacted November 21, 1991, whose findings say added remedies were needed to deter workplace harassment and intentional discrimination and which responded directly to the Supreme Court's Wards Cove decision. In between, he nominated Clarence Thomas to succeed Thurgood Marshall on the Supreme Court. The Senate confirmed Thomas 52-48 on October 15, 1991, after hearings that reopened over Anita Hill's allegations. That vote remains among the closest Supreme Court confirmations on record.

Whether the Civil Rights Act of 1991 substantially restored, or only partially restored, the standards narrowed by the Supreme Court's 1989 employment-discrimination decisions is disputed among legal scholars. The statute's own findings claim restoration; the extent is contested.

presidents.name: Bill Clinton
presidents.summary: Clinton signed the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994 and the welfare overhaul of 1996, and created the President's Advisory Board on Race by executive order in 1997. In July 2015 he told the NAACP's annual convention that he had signed a bill that made the problem worse.
presidents.paragraph: Clinton signed two laws that dominate assessments of his record. Public Law 103-322, the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, became law September 13, 1994; it funded 100,000 additional police officers and carried a federal "three strikes" life-sentence provision. Public Law 104-193, the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, became law August 22, 1996, converting cash welfare into the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant. Between them, on June 13, 1997, he issued Executive Order 13050 creating the President's Advisory Board on Race, a seven-member outside panel meant to advise on race relations, the public face of what the administration called One America. Two decades later, at the NAACP's annual meeting in Philadelphia in July 2015, Clinton said of the crime bill, "I signed a bill that made the problem worse. And I want to admit it." Both CNN and FactCheck.org report the same wording.

disputes: How much of the 1990s rise in incarceration is attributable to the 1994 federal crime bill is contested. Clinton has said the bill made the problem worse; other analysts, including FactCheck.org's review, note most incarceration growth occurred under state law rather than the federal statute. Both accounts are recorded here.

The effect of the 1996 welfare law on Black families is disputed between accounts emphasizing caseload and employment declines and accounts emphasizing deepened extreme poverty. This file records the statute, not a verdict on its effects.

presidents.name: George W. Bush
presidents.summary: Bush signed the 25-year reauthorization of the Voting Rights Act on July 27, 2006. His administration's response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005 was found deficient by a House select committee whose final report was titled "A Failure of Initiative."
presidents.paragraph: Two documented events define this stretch. Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in late August 2005 and flooded a majority-Black New Orleans. On September 15, 2005, speaking from the city, Bush said the region's deep, persistent poverty "has roots in a history of racial discrimination, which cut off generations from the opportunity of America." The following February, the House Select Bipartisan Committee to Investigate the Preparation for and Response to Hurricane Katrina transmitted its final report to the Speaker under the title "A Failure of Initiative," concluding that it had identified failures at all levels of government and that Katrina was "primarily a failure of initiative." Less than five months later, on July 27, 2006, Bush signed Public Law 109-246, the Fannie Lou Hamer, Rosa Parks, and Coretta Scott King Voting Rights Act Reauthorization and Amendments Act of 2006, whose stated purpose is to ensure the right of all citizens to vote is preserved and protected.

presidents.name: Barack Obama
presidents.summary: Obama was inaugurated January 20, 2009 as the first African American president. He signed the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010, issued the My Brother's Keeper memorandum in 2014, and his Justice Department's Civil Rights Division published its investigation of the Ferguson Police Department in March 2015.
presidents.paragraph: Obama took office January 20, 2009 as the first African American to hold the presidency. On August 3, 2010 he signed Public Law 111-220, the Fair Sentencing Act, whose text raised the crack-cocaine trigger quantities for federal mandatory minimums from 5 grams to 28 and from 50 grams to 280, cutting the 100-to-1 ratio set in 1986 to roughly 18-to-1, and eliminated the mandatory minimum for simple possession. On February 27, 2014 he signed a presidential memorandum, "Creating and Expanding Ladders of Opportunity for Boys and Young Men of Color," the founding document of My Brother's Keeper, which cited persistent gaps in employment and educational outcomes. A year later, on March 4, 2015, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division released its Ferguson investigation, reporting that African Americans made up 85 percent of vehicle stops, 90 percent of citations and 93 percent of arrests in a city that was 67 percent Black.

The reach and durability of the Justice Department's pattern-or-practice consent decrees is contested among policing scholars and municipal officials; this file records the Ferguson findings, not an assessment of the decree's results.

The Fair Sentencing Act's resulting ratio (commonly described as about 18-to-1) is an arithmetic description of the statutory quantities; the phrase "18-to-1" was not quoted from a fetched official page.

presidents.name: Donald Trump
presidents.summary: Trump signed the First Step Act on December 21, 2018 and the FUTURE Act, which made permanent mandatory funding for historically Black colleges and other minority-serving institutions, on December 19, 2019. He also signed Executive Order 13950 restricting certain diversity training by federal contractors and Executive Order 13958 creating the 1776 Commission, and his Justice Department imposed new restrictions on civil consent decrees with state and local governments.
presidents.paragraph: Four documented acts anchor this term. On December 21, 2018 Trump signed Public Law 115-391, the First Step Act of 2018, a federal sentencing and prison law whose Title I covers recidivism reduction. On December 19, 2019 he signed Public Law 116-91, the FUTURE Act, which amended the Higher Education Act to provide mandatory minority-serving-institution funding "for fiscal year 2020 and each fiscal year thereafter," replacing a program that had expired. On September 22, 2020 he issued Executive Order 13950, "Combating Race and Sex Stereotyping," applying to federal contractors, and on November 2, 2020 Executive Order 13958 established the President's Advisory 1776 Commission. Separately, Attorney General Jeff Sessions issued a November 7, 2018 memorandum setting limits on when consent decrees with state or local governments are appropriate and requiring senior-leadership approval; the Federal Register later records both that memorandum and the December 2020 rule implementing it, and their 2021-22 rescission.

disputes: The scope of the First Step Act is contested: supporters describe it as the largest federal sentencing reform in a generation, while critics note it applies only to the federal system, which holds a minority of U.S. prisoners. Both characterizations circulate; this file records the statute only.

Executive Order 13950's effect is disputed, with the administration framing it as combating stereotyping in federal contracting and civil rights organizations framing it as suppressing discussion of racism; both framings are recorded here without resolution.

Whether the November 2018 consent-decree memorandum amounted to a retreat from pattern-or-practice police oversight is a characterization; the fetched Federal Register text documents the restrictions and the later rescission, not the motive.
unverified: The Justice Department's own November 2018 press release on the Sessions memorandum could not be retrieved (justice.gov returned a bot-check page), so the memorandum is documented only through the later Federal Register descriptions.
Claims about the number of new pattern-or-practice investigations opened between 2017 and 2021 were not verified and are omitted.
The 1776 Commission's report content was not fetched and is not summarized.

presidents.name: Joe Biden
presidents.summary: Biden signed Executive Order 13985 on racial equity on his first day in office, signed the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act in June 2021 and the Emmett Till Antilynching Act in March 2022, and issued a blanket pardon for federal simple marijuana possession in October 2022. The Senate confirmed his nominee Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court on April 7, 2022.
presidents.paragraph: Biden's first official act on this front came the day he took office. Executive Order 13985, signed January 20, 2021 and published at 86 FR 7009, directs a government-wide approach to racial equity and states that entrenched disparities in laws and public policies have denied equal opportunity to individuals and communities. On June 17, 2021 he signed Public Law 117-17, adding Juneteenth National Independence Day, June 19, to the federal holiday list in 5 U.S.C. 6103. On March 29, 2022 he signed Public Law 117-107, the Emmett Till Antilynching Act, which amended 18 U.S.C. 249 to make conspiracy to commit a hate-crime offense resulting in death or serious bodily injury punishable by up to 30 years. Nine days later, on April 7, 2022, the Senate confirmed Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court, 53-47. On October 6, 2022 he issued Proclamation 10467, pardoning federal and D.C. simple marijuana possession offenses.

disputes: The practical reach of the October 2022 marijuana pardon is disputed: the proclamation covers federal and D.C. Code simple possession only, and commentators disagree about how many people it freed, since most marijuana convictions are under state law. The proclamation text is recorded; the effect estimates are not.

Whether Executive Order 13985 produced measurable changes in agency practice is contested between the administration's equity-action-plan reporting and outside critics; this file records the order, not its outcomes.
unverified: The number of people affected by the marijuana pardon proclamation was not verified from a fetched official source and is not stated.
Biden's second, broader marijuana pardon proclamation of Dec. 22, 2023 (88 FR 90083) is noted in the Federal Register index but its text was not fetched and is not described here.
